To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) decadal simulations of a climate model initialized with climate observations forced with observed volcanic forcing reproduce the pattern of near-surface temperature anomaly associated to major volcanic eruptions; 2) the contribution of initialisation to the forecast skill decreases with time; 3) the volcanic forcing is the dominant source of skill in these forecasts after the first 2-3 years, 4) a simple protocol for real time forecasts based on an exponential decay of the initial volcanic forcing allows to partially reproduce

the EC-Earth decadal forecast system initialized with observations and forced with observed volcanic aerosol forcing reproduces the observed cooling of the tropospheric temperatures in the Northern Hemisphere and the Eastern Tropical Pacific.

the EC-Earth climate model initialized with observed climate data and forced with an observed aerosol optical thickness is capable of reproducing the observed tropospheric temperature response to volcanic erufts, and that the model can be used for real-time forecasts of the tropospheric temperature anomaly induced by volcanic aerosols, using a simple protocol that involves the decay of the stratospheric aerosols.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a system for forecasting the climate response to major volcanic eruptions.

the development of an operational system for the forecast of the climate impact of volcanic eruptions, based on an estimate of the stratospheric aerosols optical depth, and the use of the EC-EARTH model to forecast the climate response.
the predictability of the response to volcanic eruption.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the forecast system has skill in reproducing the cooling associated with the volcanic eruptions in the first 2?3 years, but the forecast is less skilful than using observed forcing, especially in the first year.

the EC-Earth climate model is able to reproduce the main characteristics of the climate response to the volcanic eruptions of 1963, 1982 and 1991 and that the stratospheric forcing of these eruptions is an important source of skill in decadal climate forecasts.
the EC-Earth climate prediction system is capable of reproducing some of the climate anomalies induced by the last major volcanic eruption.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the observed stratospheric aerosols are an excellent predictor for the tropospheric temperature response to volcanic erupees, and that the EC-Earth climate model is able to reproduce the tropospheric response to volcanic erupee forcing.

, in the case of a major volcanic eruption, the climate response to the aerosol forcing can be forecasted in the first 2?3 years with skill that is comparable to that of a 2?3 year decadal forecast system initialised with climate observations.
the observed volcanic forcing is the main source of predictability for the climate response to the last major volcanic erupts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the observed volcanic forcing is a major source of skill for the prediction of the tropospheric temperature response to volcanic eruption.
the stratospheric aerosols induced by volcanic eruptions are an important source of predictability on decadal time scales.

a forecast system based on the observed stratospheric aerosols is able to reproduce the observed cooling in the first two years after a major eruption, with a skill comparable to the one obtained with the use of a past eruption.
